analysis.one_liner: Limits oil and gas futures trading to firms that actually produce, use, or take delivery of the fuel.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 121 House cosponsors, but never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: During a period of record oil and gasoline prices, this bill would have made it unlawful to trade over-the-counter derivatives on crude oil, heating oil, gasoline, or diesel fuel unless the trader was certified by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission as having the capacity to physically produce, manufacture, or take delivery of the fuel. The aim was to keep banks and financial funds from betting on energy prices, on the theory that such speculation pushes up prices for everyone at the pump. The bill went to the House Agriculture Committee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who buy gasoline, diesel, and heating oil, if limiting financial speculation actually lowered fuel prices, and businesses like trucking and airlines that buy large amounts of fuel and supported reining in speculators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, home heating customers, and fuel-heavy businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar anyone from entering into or holding an otherwise-exempt over-the-counter swap or futures contract on crude oil, heating oil, gasoline, or diesel fuel unless the Commodity Futures Trading Commission certified that the person can physically produce, manufacture, or accept delivery of that commodity.
It would not apply to regulated exchange-traded futures; it targets the largely unregulated over-the-counter swap market where financial firms were the dominant players.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, hedge funds, and other financial firms that traded large volumes of energy swaps without any connection to the physical oil or fuel market would lose their ability to do so, along with the fee income and trading profits that came with it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and hedge funds trading energy swaps

drawbacks.text: Restricting participation in derivatives markets can reduce liquidity, which some analysts argue makes prices more volatile for the very businesses the bill aimed to help; airlines and truckers hedge through these markets and would face a thinner one.

The bill covered only over-the-counter swaps and exempt transactions; trading could shift to regulated exchanges or foreign markets, and the bill's own text leaves exchange-traded futures untouched, so its effect on total speculation would be limited.
Many economists disputed that speculators, rather than supply and demand, drove the 2008 oil price spike, so the bill's main promised benefit for consumers was uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If its premise was right — that financial money in the unregulated swap market inflated fuel prices — the bill offered broad benefits to consumers at a cost concentrated on a small set of trading firms. But its narrow scope (only OTC transactions, only four fuels) and the genuine economic debate about how much speculators move prices mean the consumer benefit was less certain than its 121 cosponsors suggested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2008, sent to the House Agriculture Committee, referred to a subcommittee in November 2008, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on June 12, 2008, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day.
On November 19, 2008, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management — the last action ever taken on it.

The bill attracted 121 cosponsors, including 114 Democrats and 7 Republicans, but the Agriculture Committee never reported it and the House never voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and hedge funds that trade energy swaps kept their access to the market, and the fuel prices consumers pay were never tested against the bill's remedy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy swap dealers kept their market

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.role: U.S. Representative from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill limiting energy derivatives trading to firms with physical-market capacity.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Collin Peterson
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in June 2008 and passed it to a subcommittee in November 2008; never held a markup or advanced the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily but not entirely Democratic — 114 of 233 House Democrats and 7 of 202 House Republicans cosponsored — and since the bill never came to a vote, no roll-call ever showed where the full chamber stood.

industries.industry: Wall Street banks and hedge funds trading over-the-counter energy swaps
industries.note: These firms made money trading crude oil, gasoline, and heating oil swaps without any connection to the physical fuel market; the bill would have barred them from that market entirely unless they could take or make physical delivery. Their fee and trading income depended on the market the bill targeted.

Producers and refiners could keep trading because they can produce or take delivery of the commodity, but removing outside financial money would drain a source of buying demand that supported higher prices for their output. Their interest in maintaining that demand runs against consumers at the pump.

industries.industry: Airlines, trucking, and other large fuel buyers
industries.note: These businesses buy fuel in bulk and hedge in energy markets; if the bill lowered or stabilized fuel prices, their largest cost would fall alongside prices for ordinary drivers.
